newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says defection shows strains in N. Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says defection shows strains in N. Korea.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Thursday the defection of a top North Korean official was another sign of strains in the Stalinist country that were also reflected in food shortages and reduced military training.
Hwang Jang-yop, a member of the secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, sought refuge this week in the South Korean embassy in Beijing, leading to a diplomatic tussle over his future.
"I think it's another sign of strains in North Korea, a sign of possible strains afflicting the regime as well as the country as a whole," U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

"We already know that they are facing a hunger problem, a food shortage. We know that their training levels have been substantially below their norms for the military recently," Bacon said. U.S. defence officials say the military appears to be short of fuel.
Bacon said there was no indication of heightened military alert along the border between the two Koreas over the incident.

The State Department said it remained hopeful that the defection would not torpedo plans for a joint briefing of North Korean diplomats by U.S. and South Korean officials on a proposed four-party conference on the Korean peninsula.

"We remain hopeful that North Korea will proceed with the briefing, and get on with the four-party talks," said spokesman Nicholas Burns. "We will consider all those issues, obviously, as separate from this particular instance."

The briefing, which was to have been held in New York, has already been postponed twice by Pyongyang because of its failure so far to conclude a deal with U.S. trader Cargill Inc. to import grain to relieve its famine.

While the State Department has refused to intervene in the deal, it has said it plans to respond to a World Food Programme appeal for food aid to North Korea. Burns said a formal decision was expected soon.
Burns called the defection a "quite extraordinary event" but said he believed the United States had so far made no attempt to talk to Hwang or otherwise become involved.

"I think at this point, we're quite content to let the South Koreans and the Chinese resolve this incident," he said. "If, at some point, (Hwang) does reach South Korea or another country and wishes to talk, well, that's another matter."
